data.Question: What are Design Patterns
data.Answer: Design patterns are reusable solutions to the problems that we encounter in the day to day programming. They are generally targeted at solving the problems of object generation and integration. In other words, Design patterns acts as templates which can be applied to the real-world programming problems.

data.Question: What is the Factory Method pattern?
data.Answer: The Factory Method Pattern is a creational design pattern that provides an interface for creating objects but allows subclasses to decide which class to instantiate. This pattern promotes loose coupling by delegating object creation to a method rather than calling a constructor directly.

data.Question: What is the Abstract Factory Method pattern?
data.Answer: The Abstract Factory Pattern is a creational design pattern that provides an interface for creating families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes. It helps in managing different object creation logic without tightly coupling the implementation.

data.Question: What is the clean architecture pattern?
data.Answer: Clean architecture is a software design pattern that separates the application into distinct layers, each with its own responsibility. The goal is to create a maintainable and testable codebase by ensuring that the business logic is independent of the framework, database, and other external dependencies.

data.Question: Microservices vs Monolith
data.Answer:
AspectMonolithMicroservices
ArchitectureSingle deployable unit; all code in one codebaseMultiple independent services; each with its own codebase
DeploymentDeploy entire application for any changeDeploy individual services independently
ScalingScale entire application (vertical scaling)Scale individual services as needed (horizontal scaling)
TechnologySingle technology stackPolyglot - different tech per service
DatabaseShared databaseDatabase per service (recommended)
Team StructureSingle team or cross-functionalSmall, autonomous teams per service
ComplexitySimple to develop and debug initiallyComplex: service discovery, communication, monitoring
Failure ImpactSingle failure can bring down entire appIsolated failures; fault tolerance possible


When to use Monolith:
  • Small team or startup
  • Simple domain with limited scope
  • MVP or proof of concept
  • When you need faster initial development

When to use Microservices:
  • Large, complex domains
  • Multiple teams working independently
  • Need independent scaling of components
  • High availability requirements
  • Different parts need different technologies

Best Practice: Start with a well-structured monolith (modular monolith), then extract microservices when complexity or scaling demands it.

data.Question: Layered vs Tiered Architecture
data.Answer:
Layer = Logical separation of code (within the same application).
Tier = Physical separation of components (on different servers/machines).

AspectLayered (Logical)Tiered (Physical)
DefinitionSeparation of concerns within codeSeparation of components across machines
DeploymentAll layers deploy together as one unitEach tier can be deployed on separate servers
CommunicationIn-process method callsNetwork calls (HTTP, TCP, gRPC)
ScalingScale entire applicationScale each tier independently
PerformanceFaster (no network overhead)Network latency between tiers
ExampleUI Layer, Business Layer, Data Layer in one projectWeb Server, App Server, Database Server


Common Layers (Logical):
  • Presentation Layer: UI, Controllers, Views
  • Business Logic Layer: Services, Domain Logic
  • Data Access Layer: Repositories, EF Core, Dapper

Common Tiers (Physical):
  • 1-Tier: All on one machine (desktop app)
  • 2-Tier: Client + Database Server
  • 3-Tier: Client + App Server + Database Server
  • N-Tier: Multiple app servers, load balancers, caches

Key Point: An application can have 3 layers but run on 1 tier (single server), or have 3 layers deployed across 3 tiers (separate servers). Layers are about code organization; tiers are about deployment topology.

data.Question: What is the difference between a factory and a builder pattern?
data.Answer: The Factory pattern is used to create objects without specifying the exact class of object that will be created. It provides an interface for creating instances of a class. The Builder pattern is used to construct complex objects step by step. It allows you to create different representations of the same object.

data.Question: What is the Repository pattern?
data.Answer: The Repository pattern is a design pattern that provides a way to manage data access and storage in an application. It acts as a mediator between the domain and data mapping layers, allowing for separation of concerns and easier testing. The Repository pattern abstracts the data layer, providing a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects.

data.Question: What is difference between Unit Test and Integration Test?
data.Answer:
Unit Test

  • Tests a single unit like a method or class in isolation

  • Uses mocked dependencies

  • Very fast execution

  • Focuses on logic correctness

  • Example: testing Add(a,b) method

    • Integration Test
  • Tests multiple components working together

  • Uses real or semi-real dependencies (DB, API, services)

  • Slower execution

  • Focuses on interaction between components

  • Example: testing API → Service → Database flow

    • Key Difference
  • Unit Test = tests individual piece

  • Integration Test = tests combined system behavior

data.Question: What is Dependency Injection and how does it work in C#?
data.Answer: Dependency Injection is a design pattern used to achieve loose coupling between classes. Instead of creating dependencies inside a class using new, we inject them from outside, usually through constructor injection. In ASP.NET Core, DI is built in, and services are registered in the container with transient, scoped, or singleton lifetimes. It improves testability, maintainability, and flexibility.

data.Question: Whate are the types of Dependency Injection?
data.Answer:
1. Constructor Injection

  • Dependencies are provided through a class constructor

    • 2. Property Injection
  • Dependencies are set through public properties after object creation

    • 3. Method Injection
  • Dependencies are passed as parameters to methods when needed

    • 4. Interface Injection
  • Class implements an interface that defines a method for injecting dependencies

    • 5. Service Locator (not recommended)
  • Class retrieves dependencies from a service locator or container

data.Question: What is the difference between a Singleton and a Static class in C#?
data.Answer:
Singleton

  • Ensures only one instance of a class exists

  • Instance can implement interfaces and be passed around

  • Can have state and be garbage collected

  • Example: Logger class with instance methods

    • Static Class
  • Cannot be instantiated; all members are static

  • Cannot implement interfaces or be passed as an object

  • State is shared across all calls and cannot be garbage collected

  • Example: Math class with static methods like Math.Sqrt()

data.Question: What is the Strategy Pattern?
data.Answer:
Strategy Pattern is a behavioral design pattern that allows us to define multiple algorithms or behaviors in separate classes and choose one at runtime through a common interface. It helps remove large conditional logic and makes code more extensible and testable.

Strategy Pattern is used when we have multiple ways to perform the same action, such as different payment methods or discount calculations. We define a common interface and create separate classes for each behavior. At runtime, we select the required strategy. This avoids large if-else blocks, improves maintainability, and works very well with dependency injection in ASP.NET Core.

  • Strategy Pattern is for multiple interchangeable behaviors, uses interface + multiple implementations, removes if-else or switch complexity, supports Open/Closed Principle, and works very well with DI
